intro.text: The problem, the decisions I made, and what they produced. What is being judged here is not Swift syntax — it is technical judgement.
At Instant System, transport apps are built white-label on a shared platform.
The ticketing layer I build and maintain ships inside every one of these
— from Lyon to Tuscany, all the way to French Polynesia.

note.text: Apps published by transport authorities and their operators. My contribution covers the mobile ticketing layer — purchase, usage, validation and inspection — and its integration into each app.

intro.text: Three subjects explored properly, rather than fifteen technologies listed. These are the ones I can be challenged on for an hour.

caseStudies.title: Mobile ticketing for transport networks
caseStudies.subtitle: Instant System · since May 2023 · in production

intro.text: , alone on the ticketing scope of the whole portfolio — for a year. Here are five workstreams, each with the problem that triggered it and what it produced.

chapters.title: Authentication that logged people out for no reason
chapters.subtitle: Inherited code nobody wanted to touch — rebuilt on actors

text.text: When several requests received an unauthorised response
at the same time
, each one fired its own token refresh. The concurrent refreshes invalidated one another, and the user ended up
signed out for no apparent reason
. The authentication code dated back to 2019 and nobody wanted to touch it.
I took the initiative on the rebuild, moving to
async/await
with an
actor
holding the authentication state.
Why an actor rather than a lock:
a lock protects state provided you remember to take it everywhere — nothing checks that, and a lock held across an await is a deadlock waiting to happen. With an actor, isolation becomes a
property of the type
: every access from outside is necessarily serialised, and forgetting is no longer possible.
The heart of the fix: the
in-flight refresh task is remembered
. Concurrent requests do not start a new one, they await the same one. A single refresh, however many simultaneous calls — plus a guard against retry loops on the same call.
Authentication on TCL became markedly more stable.
No more unexplained sign-outs — the kind you never reproduce in testing and only ever see in production.

chapters.title: QR code fraud
chapters.subtitle: An innovation-sprint initiative that became a paid feature

text.text: A digital ticket is displayed as a QR code. Fraudsters would take a
screenshot
and pass it on — and at inspection, nothing told the copy apart from the original.
During an
innovation sprint
, I took the initiative of designing an internal library that
masks the screen content
as soon as a capture or a recording is under way. The ticket stays readable to its holder, and disappears from anything that could be shared.
Rolled out across
every app
, then
adopted on the new platform
. Clients are pleased with it — to the point that it became a
feature they pay for
. A sprint idea turned into a line of revenue.

chapters.title: Card top-up on the Lyon network
chapters.subtitle: From proof of concept to production, built almost single-handedly

text.text: The Lyon network had been waiting to let riders
top up a transport card from their phone
. On iOS, everything was still to be done: the ticketing vendor's SDK had never been integrated.
I first
proved the integration with a POC
— a POC should not show that it works, it should show what will break in production. Then I built
almost the entire feature on iOS single-handedly
, through to release.
Shipped. I am now
one of the technical leads on the TCL app
, which I know inside out, and I am driving the
m-ticket launch
on it.

chapters.title: Carrying clean architecture all the way
chapters.subtitle: The product owns the default, the vendor overrides only its difference

text.text: The per-vendor ticketing abstraction had been laid down by the tech lead. But implementations that were
entirely vendor-independent
still lived inside the vendor modules — duplicated once per supplier.
I
created the module for a new vendor
even though it had few specifics: keeping it outside would have been quicker, but would have left a hole in the architecture. End-to-end consistency was worth the extra code.
And I
argued for — and obtained — lifting vendor-independent implementations up to the product
. Vendors now override only what they actually mean to change.
Less duplication between suppliers, and a
clear rule that holds without arbitration
: the product owns the default behaviour, the vendor overrides only its difference.

chapters.title: Launching the new platform
chapters.subtitle: Oùra and Tuscany, across every functional area

text.text: The new product platform, in clean architecture with dependency injection, had to carry the whole of ticketing — with no regression against a platform proven over years.
I worked across
every functional area
: purchase catalogue, cart, parameterised products, purchase history, beneficiary management, buying on someone's behalf. And I wrote the
internal QR code generation library
from an encoded payload — the building block behind ticket validation and inspection.
Platform launched on
Oùra
(Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes) and in
Tuscany
. That is where I learned SwiftUI, dependency injection and this architecture —
in production, on a shipped product

caseStudies.title: KCalories — four stacks, alone, in five months
caseStudies.subtitle: Personal project · published on the App Store

text.text: I paid for three nutrition tracking apps. Price was never the obstacle —
none of them had everything
: fasting, calorie tracking, keto tracking by net carbs, and an interface you do not have to put up with.
I also wanted to find out whether I could carry a whole product, not just an iOS layer.

items.text: Build all four stacks myself
rather than assembling services: iOS app, backend, admin back-office, marketing page. Carrying the product end to end was the point, not the means.
Strict architecture and SPM modules from day one
, when nothing yet demanded it — boundaries get drawn before there is anything to put behind them, or they never get drawn at all.
Feature flags and continuous integration from week one
, to ship without blocking and without manual ritual.
Published on the App Store five months
after the first line of code.
Over 99.9% crash-free sessions
, taken from App Store Connect — above what you expect of a mobile app that runs well.
Version 2.0 twenty days
after 1.0: the delivery pipeline held.
Available in
French and English
, with two complete themes.

body.text: Session tokens, their renewal and error paths are where concurrent access produces the bugs you can never reproduce. Actors,
, isolation: what the compiler guarantees on my behalf beats what I promise to check.

Clean Architecture in separate modules rather than folders, and modules that depend on a contract, never on an implementation. A boundary the compiler does not refuse is not a boundary — it is a convention that eventually gets forgotten.

Project generation from a spec rather than a binary file, signing handled by fastlane and match, pipelines per product and per module, feature flags to decouple shipping from releasing. Whatever is not automated ends up not being done.

lede.text: A concurrency bug is not reproduced, it is reasoned about. The real question is never whether the code works, it is
what stops it from not working
— and the right answer is a compiler guarantee, not a promise kept at review time.

sections.heading: What a lock does not guarantee

text.text: A lock protects state
provided you remember to take it everywhere
. Nothing checks that: not the compiler, and not the tests, which pass for as long as the scheduling is kind to them. The day a new caller forgets, the fault shows up in production and nowhere else.
And a lock held across a suspension point is a deadlock waiting for its moment: the thread that resumes is not necessarily the one that took it.

sections.heading: Isolation as a property of the type

text.text: With an actor, isolation stops being a discipline and becomes a
property of the type
. Every access from outside is serialised by construction, and forgetting is no longer expressible — it is not a rule you apply any more, it is a compile error.
The difficulty then moves onto what crosses the boundary: whatever goes in and out must be
Sendable
. That is where the real work happens, and where you find out which of the app's types were being shared without anyone ever deciding so.

sections.heading: One remembered task rather than n tasks

text.text: The pattern reaches well beyond renewing a token:
several callers need the same result, and exactly one job should start
. The in-flight task is remembered, later callers are handed that one instead of creating another, and it is forgotten as soon as it completes.

items.text: Without it, as many failing requests trigger as many concurrent renewals — which invalidate one another.
With it, the load no longer depends on the number of callers: it depends on the number of events.
The same reasoning holds for loading a shared resource, for a migration, for warming a cache.

text.text: An actor is
not

a critical section. It is reentrant: state may have changed during a suspension, so a value read before one must be read again after. Believing otherwise swaps a race for a wrong assumption — quieter, and far slower to find.

lede.text: A boundary that rests on goodwill is not a boundary. The only question that matters is:
what fails if someone crosses it?
If the answer is a review comment, it will be crossed.

sections.heading: A folder is not a boundary

text.text: Three folders named
Domain
Data
and
Presentation
inside one target separate nothing at all: any file imports any other. The structure is there, the constraint is not — and it is the constraint that holds an architecture up, not the tree.

sections.heading: A module, on the other hand, refuses

text.text: When each layer is its own target, the rule becomes mechanical: a feature that imports the network
does not compile
. The violation no longer surfaces in review, it surfaces in red, on the machine of whoever just wrote it.

What remains is stopping the graph itself from drifting: a test reads the manifest and refuses a new dependency. Without it, the boundary holds until the day someone adds, in perfectly good faith, the line that removes it.

sections.heading: The default belongs to the product

text.text: A per-vendor abstraction is only worth something once you decide
where the shared behaviour lives
. Left inside the vendor modules, it is copied once per vendor. Lifted up to the product, it exists once, and a vendor overrides only what it actually means to change.
It is a rule that holds without arbitration: there is no discussion left about the right place, because there is only one.

Piling up abstractions is not a goal. A protocol with a single implementation you will never replace costs an indirection at every read — a senior reviewer reads that as over-engineering, not as a quality.

items.text: A port for whatever touches the outside world
: network, disk, preferences, clock.
An abstraction where it buys something
: real replaceability, testability without a simulator, or a team boundary.
Nothing elsewhere.
Knowing where to stop proves more than protocols everywhere.

lede.text: Shipping is not the last step of development, it is part of the product. Whatever stays manual ends up depending on one person and one machine — and the day either is missing, the release is not delayed, it is

sections.heading: The Xcode project is not a source file

text.text: An
.xcodeproj
is serialised state, not an intention. Two people adding a file on the same day produce a conflict you do not resolve — you arbitrate it. Generating the project from a
readable specification
makes the conflict readable again: you compare intentions, not identifiers.
Certificates installed by hand on one machine are a
hidden dependency on that machine
. Versioned and distributed, they become a project resource: any machine on the pipeline can publish, and nobody is a mandatory checkpoint any more.
A feature flag separates two decisions that get confused:
the code is in the build
and
the feature is visible
. Separating them removes the branch that lives too long, the painful merge, and the release window missed because of one feature that was not ready.

sections.heading: One pipeline per product, one per module

text.text: A published module needs its own pipeline. Without one, it is only ever validated through the app that consumes it — too late, and with the root cause buried in a project ten times its size.
That is what KCalories was there to prove at the scale of one person: the pipeline held, and the next version did not have to wait until someone found the time to publish it.

intro.text: Three codebases, three patterns, one trajectory:
MVVM on UIKit towards Clean Architecture on SwiftUI
. The counts below were measured in the repositories, not remembered — that is the only reason they are here.

patterns.name: MVC
patterns.separates: The data, its display, and the controller holding both ends.

buys.text: : it is the model UIKit hands you, and it reads without explanation. On a simple screen, it is the shortest path from intent to pixel.

costs.text: The controller becomes the only place to put whatever fits nowhere else — lifecycle, network calls, formatting, navigation. It grows, and no rule stands in its way.

chooseWhen.text: A settings screen, a fixed detail view, a prototype you will throw away.

breaksWhen.text: The moment the logic has to be tested: it lives in the controller, and the controller only exists with a loaded view.

patterns.name: MVP
patterns.separates: The decision from the display: the presenter decides, the view carries out.

buys.text: — a protocol. The logic is tested against a view double, with no simulator and no lifecycle to wake up.

costs.text: Two protocols and a hand-written refresh per screen. The presenter pushes state method by method: one forgotten call is a screen that does not update.

chooseWhen.text: A UIKit codebase where the logic must leave the controller without bringing in reactive plumbing.

breaksWhen.text: In SwiftUI: pushing state into a view that recomputes itself means working against the framework.

patterns.name: MVVM
patterns.separates: The displayable state from the view displaying it. The view observes; it is given no orders.

buys.text: rather than a sequence of calls: the view rebuilds from it, so it cannot fall out of step. It is exactly what SwiftUI expects.

costs.text: The view model attracts everything — network, formatting, navigation — until it becomes the massive controller you were fleeing, under another name.

chooseWhen.text: An app whose complexity is the interface, and whose domain holds few rules.

breaksWhen.text: When the business rule weighs more than the screen: MVVM says nothing about where it should live.

patterns.name: Clean Architecture
patterns.separates: The domain from everything else: the business rule knows nothing of the screen, the network or the store.

buys.text: . Changing the interface or the transport touches no rule, and the domain is tested without standing anything up. When the boundary is a module, it stops being a convention — the compiler refuses to cross it.

costs.text: Many more files, and a round trip per use case even when it only relays. On a trivial screen, the indirection costs more than it protects.

chooseWhen.text: A product meant to last, several teams, or several implementations behind one rule.

breaksWhen.text: When it holds by discipline rather than by the compiler: a folder named
that imports the network separates nothing.
